title: White Fang
author: Jack London
written: c. 1904–05, in California, as a deliberate companion to The Call of the Wild
setting: The Mackenzie River country of the Canadian North, Fort Yukon and Dawson in the gold-rush summer of 1898, then San Francisco and the Santa Clara Valley in California
lengthNote: Five parts and twenty-five titled chapters, about 72,000 words — more than twice the length of The Call of the Wild, and the hero is not born until the sixth chapter
openingLine: Dark spruce forest frowned on either side the frozen waterway.
summary: A cub that is three-quarters wolf is born in a cave beside a frozen stream, walks into an Indian camp, and spends the rest of the book being made into whatever his owners need: a sled dog for Grey Beaver, a pit fighter for Beauty Smith, and at last a house dog for a mining expert’s family in California. London sets out to prove that character is clay pressed by circumstance, and he is thorough enough to apply the same rule to a camp cook and an escaped convict. The difficulty the novel never quite settles is that its happy ending is also a surrender, and that the thumb which finally presses the wolf into a fairer shape belongs to a man he calls a god.

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of White Fang
sourceText.note: The novel is divided into five parts, and the chapter numbers begin again in each. Parts and chapters carry Roman numerals and titles in the text; they are cited here by Arabic numeral, as Part 3, Chapter 2.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Serialised in Outing magazine from May to October, then issued as a book by Macmillan in the same autumn.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: The Wild, the cave, the Indian camp, the white men of the Yukon, and California: each part is a new owner or a new law.

atAGlance.label: Companion to
atAGlance.note: Buck goes from a judge’s estate in the Santa Clara Valley to the wolves; White Fang goes from the wolves to a judge’s estate in the same valley.

atAGlance.label: Parentage
atAGlance.note: His father, One Eye, is a wolf; his mother, Kiche, is the daughter of a wolf and an Indian camp dog, which is why she answers to her name.

structure.label: Part 1
structure.title: The Wild
structure.summary: Two men, six dogs and a coffin are followed down a frozen river by a starving wolf pack that takes the dogs one by one, lured out by a she-wolf who knows the ways of camps. White Fang is not yet born. The part exists to show the Wild from the position of the meat, so that every later chapter about a hunting cub is read by someone who has already been hunted.

scenes.title: The Trail of the Meat
scenes.summary: Bill and Henry haul the body of Lord Alfred towards Fort McGurry; Bill feeds seven dogs where there should be six, and in the morning Fatty is gone.

scenes.title: The She-Wolf
scenes.summary: Frog and Spanker are taken, the she-wolf shows herself in daylight and decoys One Ear from the traces, and Bill goes after her with three cartridges and does not come back.

scenes.title: The Hunger Cry
scenes.summary: Henry, alone with two dogs, slings the coffin into a tree and holds the pack off from inside a ring of fire until a party of men finds him asleep in the ashes.

structure.label: Part 2
structure.title: Born of the Wild
structure.summary: The pack breaks up, old One Eye wins the she-wolf by killing his rivals, and a litter is born in a cave above a stream. Famine leaves one grey cub alive. He learns fear before he has met anything to be afraid of, tumbles out through the wall of light into a world of ptarmigan, hawks and weasels, and arrives at a law in three words.

scenes.title: The Battle of the Fangs
scenes.summary: The famine ends, the pack divides, and One Eye and a young leader together kill an ambitious three-year-old before One Eye kills the young leader as well.

scenes.title: The Lair
scenes.summary: The she-wolf finds a cave and whelps; One Eye waits out a porcupine and a lynx and carries home what the lynx leaves.

scenes.title: The Grey Cub
scenes.summary: The one grey cub of the litter takes the cave mouth for a wall of light; a second famine kills his brothers and sisters, and the lynx kills his father.

scenes.title: The Wall of the World
scenes.summary: He falls through the wall, eats a nest of ptarmigan chicks, is beaten by the hen, nearly drowned in a stream and nearly killed by a weasel.

scenes.title: The Law of Meat
scenes.summary: The she-wolf robs the lynx’s lair, the lynx comes for the cave, and mother and cub kill her between them; the cub draws the conclusion.

structure.label: Part 3
structure.title: The Gods of the Wild
structure.summary: The cub meets five Indians on the way to the stream, his mother crawls to them at the sound of her name, and he is named and owned in a single speech. In Grey Beaver’s camp he learns clubs, fire, laughter, property and the sled, is made an outcast by the puppy pack under Lip-lip, and comes back of his own accord when he might have stayed wild.

scenes.title: The Makers of Fire
scenes.summary: Grey Beaver recognises Kiche, names the cub and claims him; White Fang meets Lip-lip, burns his nose on a fire, and is laughed at.

scenes.title: The Bondage
scenes.summary: Kiche is handed to Three Eagles to settle a debt, and White Fang, swimming after her canoe, takes his first real beating and learns never to bite a god.

scenes.title: The Outcast
scenes.summary: Lip-lip turns every young dog in the camp against him, and he learns to fight without warning and to go for the throat.

scenes.title: The Trail of the Gods
scenes.summary: He hides when the camp moves in the autumn, finds that freedom is cold and silent, and runs forty hours down the river bank to crawl to Grey Beaver’s fire.

scenes.title: The Covenant
scenes.summary: Harnessed in Mit-sah’s team behind a persecuted Lip-lip, he learns what property is, and defends Mit-sah against a gang of boys.

scenes.title: The Famine
scenes.summary: He faces down old Baseek over a shin-bone, is slashed by a mother who has forgotten him, lives wild through the famine, kills Lip-lip, and goes back to the village.

structure.label: Part 4
structure.title: The Superior Gods
structure.summary: Made sled leader and hated for it, he travels with Grey Beaver to Fort Yukon in the summer of 1898 and is sold for whisky to Beauty Smith, who turns him into the Fighting Wolf. A bulldog he cannot throw gets him by the throat, and a young mining expert pulls the jaws apart, buys him by force and begins, with great patience, to unmake what the pit has made.

scenes.title: The Enemy of His Kind
scenes.summary: Running at the head of a team that wants to tear him down, he crosses the Rockies to Fort Yukon and sees his first white men.

scenes.title: The Mad God
scenes.summary: Beauty Smith, the fort’s cook, buys him from a drunk Grey Beaver with bottles; he gnaws free twice and is twice handed back and beaten.

scenes.title: The Reign of Hate
scenes.summary: Caged, goaded and exhibited at Dawson, he fights dogs, wolves and a full-grown lynx, and never loses his feet.

scenes.title: The Clinging Death
scenes.summary: Tim Keenan’s bulldog Cherokee gets a grip and keeps it; Weedon Scott knocks Beauty Smith down, levers the jaws open with a revolver and pays a hundred and fifty dollars.

scenes.title: The Indomitable
scenes.summary: He kills a sled dog and lays open Scott’s hand, and is reprieved because he knows what a rifle is and has the sense to get out of its way.

scenes.title: The Love-Master
scenes.summary: Scott’s hand comes down without hurting; liking becomes love; White Fang sickens when Scott goes away, and mauls Beauty Smith when he comes to steal him.

structure.label: Part 5
structure.title: The Tame
structure.summary: He breaks through a cabin window to follow Scott aboard the steamer and is taken to the Scott family estate in California, where he has to learn that chickens, cats, children and other dogs are all under the protection of the gods. He pays for his place by killing the convict who comes for the Judge, and ends the book in the sun with puppies climbing on him.

scenes.title: The Long Trail
scenes.summary: Locked in the cabin, he goes through the window and is waiting on the deck of the Aurora; Scott gives in.

scenes.title: The Southland
scenes.summary: San Francisco appals him, a baggage car carries him south, and at Sierra Vista he is met by a deer-hound and by a sheepdog, Collie, who knows a wolf when she sees one.

scenes.title: The God’s Domain
scenes.summary: He learns the household, kills fifty Leghorn hens in one night, is taught better, and wins Scott a bet against the Judge by sitting an afternoon in the chicken yard.

scenes.title: The Call of Kind
scenes.summary: He learns to be laughed at, fetches help when Scott’s horse falls and breaks his leg, barking for the only time in his life, and runs in the woods with Collie.

scenes.title: The Sleeping Wolf
scenes.summary: Jim Hall escapes from San Quentin to kill the Judge who sentenced him; White Fang kills him on the stairs, takes three bullets, and is named the Blessed Wolf.

characters.name: White Fang
characters.role: A wolf-dog, three parts wolf: sled dog, pit fighter, house dog
characters.summary: He is the only survivor of his litter and the quickest learner in every company he enters, and what he learns depends entirely on who has hold of him. The book is careful to make him neither noble nor vicious by nature: he is morose and murderous under Lip-lip and Beauty Smith and devoted under Scott, and London’s point is that it is the same animal each time.
characters.clue: Named in a single sentence by an Indian who has just clouted him, this one never barks but twice in his life, fights without warning, and ends by letting puppies climb over him in the California sun.

characters.name: Kiche, the she-wolf
characters.role: White Fang’s mother; half wolf, half Indian camp dog
characters.summary: In Part 1 she is the red-hued decoy who lures sled dogs out of camp to be eaten, and in Part 2 a fierce and competent mother; in Part 3 she drops to her belly at the sound of her own name. She is the book’s first proof that a creature can belong to the Wild and to men by turns, and her forgetting of her son is given as a plain fact of wolf-motherhood rather than a wound.
characters.clue: She knows enough about campfires to steal from them and enough about men to come when they call her; a year after losing her cub she lays his cheek open to the bone.

characters.name: One Eye
characters.role: An old grey wolf, White Fang’s father
characters.summary: A scarred veteran who runs on the she-wolf’s blind side and wins her by patience and by treachery, killing a rival while the rival is licking a wound. He is a dutiful provider who is rather afraid of his mate, and he dies offstage, killed by the lynx, leaving only the remains his mate finds at the end of his trail.
characters.clue: He has lost the sight on one side and most of his illusions, waits an hour beside a rolled-up porcupine because something may happen, and is found at last as a few remains near a lynx’s lair.

characters.name: Grey Beaver
characters.role: A Mackenzie Indian, White Fang’s first master
characters.summary: He is just by his own lights, never caresses and never beats without cause, and defends his dog against the whole camp when it has killed another man’s. What he offers is a bargain — food, fire and protection for work and obedience — and the novel respects the bargain while insisting it contains no love. Whisky undoes him at Fort Yukon, and he sells for bottles what he had refused to sell for dollars.
characters.clue: He names a cub in one breath and clouts it in the next, holds the door of his tepee against an angry camp, and in the end trades the best sled dog on the Mackenzie for something in a black bottle.

characters.name: Lip-lip
characters.role: A camp puppy, older and larger than White Fang
characters.summary: A bully who wins his first fight with the newcomer and makes a career of it, leading the puppy pack against White Fang until the cub has no companion in the camp but his tied-up mother. The narrator holds him responsible for a good deal: without him, we are told, White Fang might have grown up more doglike and more liking of dogs.
characters.clue: He had fought many puppy fights before the stranger arrived and enjoyed winning them; years later, thin with famine, he meets that stranger alone at the foot of a bluff.

characters.name: Beauty Smith
characters.role: Cook and drudge at Fort Yukon; owner of the Fighting Wolf
characters.summary: Misshapen, cowardly and cruel, he takes out on a caged animal what stronger men have done to him. London describes him at cruel length and then pronounces him not responsible, since the clay of him was moulded that way in the making. The verdict is consistent with the book’s theory, though the chapter’s evident loathing of him is not.
characters.clue: The other men gave him his first name as a joke; he cooks for them, is feared for what he might put in the coffee, and laughs when the thing in the cage goes mad with hate.
traits: patient in getting what he wants

relationships.label: is knocked down and bought out by

characters.name: Weedon Scott
characters.role: A mining expert from California; the love-master
characters.summary: He arrives in the book as a fist in Beauty Smith’s face and then turns out to be its gentlest figure, undertaking the taming as a debt — a way, he thinks, of redeeming mankind from the wrong it had done the dog. He is also a judge’s son with money and connections, and the ease with which he overrides another man’s property rights is something the novel enjoys rather than examines.
characters.clue: He pays a hundred and fifty dollars for a half-dead dog whose owner is not selling, has his hand laid open for his trouble, and sits down on the cabin step next day to try again.

relationships.label: rescues, tames and is loved by

characters.name: Matt
characters.summary: The practical man of Part 4, who spots the harness marks on White Fang’s chest, argues for giving him a chance, and feeds him for months without ever being accepted as his master. His slangy commentary keeps the taming chapters from turning solemn, and his puzzlement that the dog should love the man who never feeds him is the book’s own question put in plain speech.
characters.clue: He tells his employer to his face that he is seventeen kinds of a fool, and shouts from a gang-plank that the wolf will never stand the climate unless he is clipped.

characters.name: Collie
characters.summary: She alone refuses the household’s verdict on the newcomer: generations of guarding flocks tell her what he is, and she nags, nips and shoulders him for months. She is right, as the chicken-yard shows, and the novel lets her be right and lose. By the last chapter she has a litter by the ancient marauder and is still snarling at him.
characters.clue: Her instinct is older than her manners; she drives the newcomer across the fields after the business with the groom, and a season later runs beside him in the woods as another female once ran beside One Eye.

characters.name: Judge Scott
characters.role: Weedon Scott’s father, master of Sierra Vista
characters.summary: A genial retired judge who bets that a chicken-killer cannot be cured and cheerfully pays up when he is. He is also the man who, in good faith and on perjured evidence, sent Jim Hall to prison for fifty years, so the comfortable household that receives White Fang rests on exactly the kind of mistaken sentence the novel has been arguing against.
characters.clue: He must say sixteen times, slowly and solemnly, that the wolf is smarter than he thought; he pooh-poohs the newspapers, though not with reason.

characters.name: Jim Hall
characters.role: A convict escaped from San Quentin
characters.summary: He enters five chapters from the end and is given, in two pages, the same life as the hero: soft clay handled harshly, a cage, a keeper who was as great a beast as he, and teeth used on a throat. The difference is that nobody comes for him. He is innocent of the crime he was sentenced for, and the dog who was saved kills the man who was not.
characters.clue: He was a little pulpy boy in a city slum, lived three years in an iron cell without seeing the sky, and crept one night up a judge’s staircase past something asleep in the hall.

relationships.label: the human double of, killed by

characters.name: Bill and Henry
characters.role: Two dog-drivers carrying a coffin to Fort McGurry
characters.summary: They own Part 1 and then vanish from the book. Bill frets, counts dogs and cartridges and finally goes after the pack with a rifle; Henry eats his beans, reproves him for being off colour, and survives. Their laconic talk across the fire is London’s way of measuring how near death is without having to say so.
characters.clue: One of them counts seven dogs at feeding time when there should be six; the other ends up asleep inside a circle of embers with his mittens burnt through.

themes.name: The clay and the thumb
themes.summary: London states his thesis outright and repeats it at every change of owner: heredity is a life-stuff like clay, and environment is what models it. The cub who would have become a true wolf becomes a wolfish dog, then a fiend in a cage, then a guardian of children, without his nature changing at all. The argument is applied even-handedly to human beings, which is where it becomes uncomfortable.
themes.development: Announced in Part 3, Chapter 6; extended to Beauty Smith, who is pronounced not responsible, in Part 4; turned into the thumb of circumstance, which is Weedon Scott, in Part 4, Chapter 6; and closed with Jim Hall, the soft clay of a San Francisco slum, in the last chapter.

themes.name: Gods, clubs and the power of dead things
themes.summary: White Fang’s theology is strictly empirical. Men are gods because sticks and stones fly at their bidding, because they make fire, and later because they make steamboats and cable cars; the more power, the higher the god. The scheme lets London describe domination from underneath, as something felt to be in the order of things, and it means that every beating in the book is also an act of worship.
themes.development: First felt as the man-animals’ mastery over dead things in Part 3; ranked, with white men above Indians, at Fort Yukon in Part 4; pushed to the point of terror on the pavement of San Francisco; and domesticated at Sierra Vista, where the gods’ power shows chiefly in what they forbid.

themes.name: Eat or be eaten
themes.summary: The Wild of this novel is a food chain with no outside. Part 1 shows it from the point of view of two men being eaten, Part 2 from that of a cub learning to eat, and the narrator is explicit that the cub lives the law without ever thinking it. What follows in the camps and the fighting pit is the same law with men added, which is London’s reason for starting where he does.
themes.development: The pack runs down the sled team in Part 1; the cub kills ptarmigan chicks and is nearly killed by a weasel in Part 2; the code becomes obey the strong and oppress the weak in the camp; and in California he must unlearn it hen by hen.

themes.name: The covenant: liberty for a god
themes.summary: The central bargain of the book is put in contractual terms: food, fire, protection and companionship on one side; work, obedience and the guarding of property on the other, with liberty as the price. London calls it the ancient covenant of the first wolf that came in from the Wild, and he is honest that it is a relief as well as a loss, since it is easier to lean upon another than to stand alone.
themes.development: Kiche crawls to her name; White Fang comes in to Grey Beaver’s fire of his own choice in Part 3, Chapter 4; the terms are set out in Chapter 5; whisky breaks the contract from the god’s side in Part 4; and under Scott the same service is rendered for love rather than awe.

themes.name: Like replaced by love
themes.summary: For three parts the best feeling available to White Fang is liking, and the book says flatly that his service to Grey Beaver had no love in it because he did not know what love was. Scott’s hand, which comes down and does not hurt, reaches a capacity that had nearly died. The love that results is exclusive, jealous of its dignity, and expressed by a growl with a crooning note in it.
themes.development: Absent in the Indian camp; awakened against every instinct in Part 4, Chapter 6; proved by the broken window and the pining when Scott is away; and tested in the South, where he must extend a grudging tolerance to everyone the master loves.

themes.name: The enemy of his kind
themes.summary: White Fang belongs to no pack after the cave. The puppies reject him as a wolf, the sled team hates him as a leader, the fighting pit makes every dog an opponent, and he learns to want only to be let alone. London treats this solitude as manufactured, not natural, and the measure of his recovery at the end is that he can lie still while another animal’s young climb over him.
themes.development: Lip-lip’s persecution in Part 3; the leader’s place at the head of a team that wants to pull him down in Part 4; the cage; then Dick’s rebuffed overtures and Collie’s long hostility in Part 5, ending with the puppies in the stable doorway.

themes.name: Who is responsible
themes.summary: If character is pressed into shape from outside, blame becomes hard to place, and the novel knows it. The narrator excuses Beauty Smith, indicts society for Jim Hall, and shows a kindly judge passing a fifty-year sentence on perjured evidence. Yet Beauty Smith is still punched and Jim Hall is still killed, and the household applauds. The book’s theory and its sense of what is deserved never quite meet.
themes.development: Grey Beaver’s rough fairness in the camp is called justice and felt as such; Scott tells Beauty Smith he has forfeited his rights; and the last chapter sets a railroaded man against the dog, with the reader’s sympathy deliberately divided.

techniques.name: The animal point of view
techniques.definition: Narration tied to the perceptions of a creature that cannot use language, so that thought has to be shown as sensation, memory and behaviour.
techniques.inThisBook: The cave mouth is a wall of light, men are man-animals and then gods, a cable car is a screaming lynx. The narrator keeps marking the limit — had the cub thought in man-fashion, which he did not — so that the theory belongs to London and only the experience to the wolf.

techniques.name: The returning phrase
techniques.definition: A phrase repeated at intervals so that its meaning changes with each context.
techniques.inThisBook: The clay comes back at least a dozen times: the clay of his nature, the clay of Beauty Smith, the plasticity of his clay, soft clay in the hands of society. Each return widens the claim, until a figure introduced to explain a puppy is being used to indict a prison system.

techniques.name: Grand diction for animal experience
techniques.definition: Deliberately heightened, Latinate vocabulary applied to creatures and events that would ordinarily be described plainly.
techniques.inThisBook: A dog’s submission is written as theology — gods, altars, covenant, allegiance, fealty — and a nest of ptarmigan chicks leads to a paragraph on a chaos of gluttony and slaughter, merciless, planless, endless. The register insists that nothing here is merely an animal story.

techniques.name: The Wild as an adversary
techniques.definition: Using terrain, weather and scale to exert force on the characters rather than to decorate them.
techniques.inThisBook: The opening page gives the Northland a will: it laughs, it hates movement, it freezes water to stop it running. California, by contrast, is all fences, porches and chicken-yards, and its pressure on White Fang is a matter of rules rather than cold.

techniques.name: Dialect
techniques.inThisBook: Bill, Henry and Matt speak a clipped frontier slang — I’m jes’ plump tuckered out — while Grey Beaver is given a formal, almost biblical English and then, to the white man, a trader’s pidgin. The narrator alone has the vocabulary of science, which places every speaker beneath the explanation of his own behaviour.

techniques.name: Foils and doubles
techniques.definition: A character constructed to throw another’s choices into relief by making different ones.
techniques.inThisBook: Lip-lip is the dog White Fang might have been in a friendlier camp; Cherokee is patience against speed; Collie is instinct that cannot be talked round; and Jim Hall is White Fang without a Weedon Scott, which is why the two are brought together on a staircase in the dark.

techniques.name: An opening without the hero
techniques.definition: Beginning a narrative with characters and events that the main story will leave behind, so that the protagonist enters a world the reader already fears.
techniques.inThisBook: Part 1 is a self-contained tale of two men eaten out of their dog team, and neither man is heard of again. Its purpose is positional: the reader meets White Fang’s mother as a killer of dogs before meeting her as a mother, and knows what the Wild does to meat before a cub is asked to learn it.

quotations.text: Dark spruce forest frowned on either side the frozen waterway.
quotations.context: The novel’s opening sentence.
quotations.analysis: The forest is given a face before any living thing appears, and the missing preposition — either side the waterway, not either side of it — gives the line a faintly archaic stiffness that suits a landscape about to be credited with wisdom and malice. The waterway is frozen: the first thing the reader learns about this country is that it has stopped something moving.

quotations.text: It is not the way of the Wild to like movement. Life is an offence to it, for life is movement; and the Wild aims always to destroy movement.
quotations.context: The narrator, having described two men and a dog team hauling a coffin down the frozen river.
quotations.analysis: Life is defined here as movement and nothing more, which is a naturalist’s definition and leaves out everything a reader would ordinarily call character. The definition matters later: the cub’s joy is the play of his muscles, the bulldog’s grip kills by stopping motion, and White Fang’s cage is a torment because it does to him what the Wild does to water.

quotations.text: They reminded him of children gathered about a spread table and awaiting permission to begin to eat. And he was the food they were to eat!
quotations.context: Henry, alone by his fire, looking at the ring of wolves sitting in the snow around him.
quotations.analysis: The simile is domestic and almost fond, and it is the man’s own; his mind reaches for a nursery to describe his death. It also states the position from which the rest of the book must be read. Before a wolf is ever made sympathetic, the reader has sat where the meat sits and seen the patience of the pack from inside the circle.

quotations.text: So to him the entrance of the cave was a wall—a wall of light.
quotations.context: The grey cub, who has never left the lair and has no idea that there is an outside.
quotations.analysis: London solves the problem of an animal’s ignorance by giving the cub a wrong idea that is perfectly reasonable: every other side of his world is a wall, so the bright side must be one too. The dash makes the reader arrive at the image a beat late, as the cub does. When he later falls through it, the book has its model for every subsequent change of world.

quotations.text: Fear!—that legacy of the Wild which no animal may escape nor exchange for pottage.
quotations.context: The narrator explains why a cub that has never met anything dangerous is nevertheless afraid to approach the cave mouth.
quotations.analysis: This is the heredity half of the book’s equation, and it is put in the language of inheritance law: a legacy, passed down through a thousand thousand lives. The allusion to Esau’s mess of pottage is characteristic. London reaches for Genesis to describe a wolf cub’s nerves, and the point of the allusion is that this birthright, unlike Esau’s, cannot be sold.

quotations.text: The aim of life was meat. Life itself was meat. Life lived on life. There were the eaters and the eaten. The law was: EAT OR BE EATEN.
quotations.context: After the fight in which the she-wolf and the cub kill the lynx, the cub begins to hunt beside his mother.
quotations.analysis: Five sentences, each shorter than a line, with meat and life exchanging places until they are the same word. The capitals are the only ones of their kind in the novel and give the law the look of a notice nailed to a wall. It is worth setting beside the law of club and fang in the earlier book: that law was taught by men, while this one needs nobody to teach it.

quotations.text: He did not even think the law; he merely lived the law without thinking about it at all.
quotations.context: The narrator’s immediate gloss on the law of meat.
quotations.analysis: Having stated the law in capitals, London at once takes it away from the animal it describes. The sentence is a defence prepared in advance against the charge that he gives beasts human reasoning: the formulating is the author’s, the living is the cub’s. It also describes most of the human characters, none of whom could state the rules they act on.

quotations.text: His fangs be white, and White Fang shall be his name. I have spoken. He is my dog.
quotations.speaker: Grey Beaver
quotations.context: Grey Beaver has recognised Kiche as his dead brother’s dog and has his hand on her cub.
quotations.analysis: Naming and owning happen in the same breath, and the cub who was the grey cub for five chapters gets a name only at the moment he becomes property. The ceremonial English London gives Grey Beaver makes the claim sound like a legal finding, which in the camp it is: the title to the dog descends through the mother and the dead brother, and nobody disputes it.

quotations.text: They enforced their live strength with the power of dead things. Dead things did their bidding.
quotations.context: The cub watches the Indians drive off the camp dogs with clubs and stones.
quotations.analysis: This is a definition of the human from outside the species: not speech or reason but the tool, seen as sorcery. Live and dead are set against each other twice in two sentences. It is the ground of everything White Fang later believes about gods, and it explains why the white men rank higher, since their dead things are steamboats.

quotations.text: He turned and fled away, not from the hurt of the fire, but from the laughter that sank even deeper, and hurt in the spirit of him.
quotations.context: The cub has burnt his nose and tongue on Grey Beaver’s fire, and the whole camp is laughing at him.
quotations.analysis: London gives his animal shame on the first day among men, and admits in the next breath that it is not given us to know how animals know laughter. Ridicule remains White Fang’s sorest point: the crowds at the cage laugh, Beauty Smith laughs. The measure of Scott’s achievement in Part 5 is a single detail, that the dog learns to be laughed at by him and to laugh back.

quotations.text: There it stands, on its two hind-legs, club in hand, immensely potential, passionate and wrathful and loving, god and mystery and power all wrapped up and around by flesh that bleeds when it is torn and that is good to eat like any flesh.
quotations.context: The narrator on why the wolf and the wild dog, unlike man, never lose faith in their gods.
quotations.analysis: The sentence builds a deity and then eats it. Hind-legs sees man from the ground; the abstractions pile up in the manner of a creed; and the last clause returns the god to the food chain of Part 2. The joke is at the expense of human religion, whose gods are vapours and mists, but it also keeps the reader from sentimentalising the dog’s devotion: what is worshipped here is a club.

quotations.text: This in itself was compensation, for it is always easier to lean upon another than to stand alone.
quotations.context: White Fang is learning that his body is the man-animals’ to command, and finding, unknown to himself, that he likes it.
quotations.analysis: The narrator slips from the past tense of the story into a present-tense maxim, and the maxim is not about dogs. London was a socialist writing about the attractions of submission, and he is candid that handing over the responsibilities of existence is a pleasure as well as a defeat. The Call of the Wild has no equivalent sentence; this is the companion book’s distinct subject.

quotations.text: Of his own choice, he came in to sit by man’s fire and to be ruled by him.
quotations.context: Having hidden in the woods when the camp moved, and found freedom lonely, White Fang has tracked Grey Beaver down and crawls to his feet expecting a beating.
quotations.analysis: The sentence that most exactly reverses Buck’s story. The door to the Wild was open, and the phrase of his own choice is placed first so it cannot be missed. Fire and rule arrive together in one clause, comfort and government as a single offer. What he gets, instead of the blow, is half a lump of tallow, which is the book’s first act of kindness and costs Grey Beaver almost nothing.

quotations.text: For the possession of a flesh-and-blood god, he exchanged his own liberty.
quotations.context: The narrator sets out the terms of the covenant between dog and man.
quotations.analysis: Possession is a pointed word, since it is the dog who is possessed; London lets him think of himself as the one acquiring something. The grammar of exchange runs through the whole paragraph — received, in return — so that domestication reads as a contract freely entered. The next paragraph adds the clause that matters for Part 4: it was a service of duty and awe, but not of love.

quotations.text: His heredity was a life-stuff that may be likened to clay. It possessed many possibilities, was capable of being moulded into many different forms.
quotations.context: The narrator takes stock of White Fang at the end of the Indian-camp chapters.
quotations.analysis: The novel’s thesis, stated as a simile and in the hedged voice of a lecture: may be likened to. Its importance is what it refuses. There is no wolf nature that must come out in the end and no dog nature either; there are possibilities, and then there is pressure. Everything that follows — the fighting pit, the taming, the convict — is offered as an experiment on this proposition.

quotations.text: There was no place for her in his scheme of things, as there was no place for him in hers.
quotations.context: White Fang meets Kiche again; she has a new litter, does not know him, and lays his cheek open.
quotations.analysis: The balanced clauses hand out the indifference equally and refuse the reunion a sentimental reader has been waiting for since the canoe carried her off. London’s explanation is zoological — a wolf-mother is not made to remember — and the effect is to leave White Fang with no tie that was not made by a man. The covenant chapter has just told us he would not have left his god for her anyway.

quotations.text: In short, Beauty Smith was a monstrosity, and the blame of it lay elsewhere. He was not responsible. The clay of him had been so moulded in the making.
quotations.context: The end of a long physical description of the Fort Yukon cook who wants to buy White Fang.
quotations.analysis: The clay figure is transferred from dog to man without any change of wording, and that is the test of whether London means it. He does, in theory: three flat sentences acquit the villain before he has done anything. But the preceding page has read cowardice off a jaw and cruelty off a forehead with obvious relish, so the chapter both excuses Beauty Smith and invites the reader to be revolted by him.

quotations.text: They were his environment, these men, and they were moulding the clay of him into a more ferocious thing than had been intended by Nature.
quotations.context: White Fang in a cage on the steamboat to Dawson, poked with sticks by men who then laugh at him.
quotations.analysis: Environment, up to now a matter of snow, famine and other dogs, is redefined as spectators. The crowd at the bars is not watching a fierce animal but making one, and a paragraph later London adds that the ferocity fed upon itself because everyone treated him as ferocious. Intended by Nature is a rare lapse into purpose in a book that otherwise allows Nature no intentions at all.

quotations.text: “A man’s got his rights. But you’re not a man. You’re a beast.”
quotations.speaker: Weedon Scott
quotations.context: Scott forces a hundred and fifty dollars on Beauty Smith, who protests that he has his rights and is not selling.
quotations.analysis: The scene is written to be cheered, and it should also be noticed. Scott agrees that a man has rights and then removes Beauty Smith from the category, which is precisely the move the novel’s theory forbids: two chapters earlier the narrator ruled that this man was not responsible. Beast is the book’s most unstable word, used with contempt here, of a convict later, and of its hero never.

quotations.text: “If you don’t mind my expressin’ my feelin’s, Mr. Scott, I’ll make free to say you’re seventeen kinds of a damn fool an’ all of ’em different, an’ then some.”
quotations.speaker: Matt
quotations.context: Matt comes out of the cabin with a pan of dishwater and finds his employer patting the dog that tore his hand open the day before.
quotations.analysis: The taming is the emotional centre of the book, and London protects it from solemnity by having it watched by a man with a dishpan. Matt’s elaborate courtesy before the insult marks the distance between hired man and mining expert, and his seventeen comes back at the chapter’s end, when Beauty Smith is said to have thought he had hold of seventeen devils.

quotations.text: Yet again, in this new orientation, it was the thumb of circumstance that pressed and prodded him, softening that which had become hard and remoulding it into fairer form. Weedon Scott was in truth this thumb.
quotations.context: The narrator on what the change from the reign of hate required of a grown animal whose fibre had become tough and knotty.
quotations.analysis: London will not allow even the redemption to be an exception to his rule. Kindness is not a moral force entering a mechanical world; it is one more thumb, and Scott is an environment like Lip-lip or the cage. The short second sentence, a man identified as a digit, is almost comic in its literalness, and it is the most rigorous thing in the book.

quotations.text: And love was the plummet dropped down into the deeps of him where like had never gone.
quotations.context: White Fang has begun to wait for hours on the cabin stoop for a sight of Scott, and to go without meat to be with him.
quotations.analysis: A plummet is a sounding lead: love here is an instrument for finding depth, and the claim is that the depth was already there. That sits oddly beside the clay, which has no depths, only surfaces to be pressed, and the tension is real. When London wants to say what Scott did, he uses a thumb; when he wants to say what White Fang felt, he has to give him an inside.

quotations.text: And never had the white men seemed such marvellous gods as now, when he trod the slimy pavement of San Francisco.
quotations.context: White Fang lands from the steamer among waggons, automobiles and cable cars.
quotations.analysis: The adjective undercuts the awe. White Fang’s scale of godhead rises with every display of power over matter, and the city is the greatest display yet; but the pavement the gods have made is slimy, and the cars screech like the lynxes of his cubhood. London had no love for cities, and lets the wolf register one as the Wild’s terrors rebuilt in iron.

quotations.text: And the chief thing demanded by these intricacies of civilisation was control, restraint—a poise of self that was as delicate as the fluttering of gossamer wings and at the same time as rigid as steel.
quotations.context: Life in the Santa Clara Valley after the simplicities of the Northland: butcher’s meat he must not touch, cats he must let alone, boys who throw stones.
quotations.analysis: Civilisation is defined by what it forbids, and the definition is not flattering: the tame life asks for more self-suppression than the sled ever did. Gossamer and steel are an odd pair for a wolf, and the strain in the simile is the strain it describes. This is the sentence to set against any reading of Part 5 as a simple reward.

quotations.text: It was the treatment he had received from the time he was a little pulpy boy in a San Francisco slum—soft clay in the hands of society and ready to be formed into something.
quotations.context: The narrator’s account of Jim Hall, for whom strait-jackets, starvation and beatings were the wrong treatment.
quotations.analysis: The refrain’s last appearance, and its most political. Every term used of the cub is reused: soft, clay, hands, formed. Pulpy is the unexpected word, making the child unpleasant and defenceless at once. London then has his rescued animal tear out the throat of his unrescued man, and lets the household call it a blessing, which is either a failure of nerve or the bleakest irony in the book.

quotations.text: This passed away as the puppies’ antics and mauling continued, and he lay with half-shut patient eyes, drowsing in the sun.
quotations.context: The novel’s last sentence: the convalescent White Fang in the stable doorway, with Collie’s puppies clambering over him to the applause of the gods.
quotations.analysis: The book that began with frost, dusk and a land hostile to movement ends with a wolf lying still in sunlight by his own consent. Mauling is the right word, recalling every mauling he has taken, now harmless. Whether this is fulfilment or extinction is left to the reader: Buck ends singing at the head of a pack, and White Fang ends half asleep with an audience.

timeline.label: Jack London born in San Francisco
timeline.detail: He grew up poor around Oakland and the bay, the city whose slums he gives to Jim Hall.

timeline.label: London goes north to the Klondike
timeline.detail: He wintered in the Yukon in the first season of the rush and came home the following summer with scurvy and notebooks rather than gold.

timeline.label: The summer the novel names
timeline.detail: White Fang reaches Fort Yukon in the summer of 1898, with thousands of gold-hunters going upriver to Dawson — the only calendar date in the book.

timeline.label: The Call of the Wild published
timeline.detail: Its success fixed London’s public identity and created the appetite for a second dog book.

timeline.label: London buys land at Glen Ellen
timeline.detail: The beginning of the Sonoma ranch where he lived for the rest of his life; the novel’s Californian chapters were written by a man settling into the country himself.

timeline.label: White Fang serialised and published
timeline.detail: Six monthly instalments in Outing from May to October, then the Macmillan book with colour plates by Charles Livingston Bull.

timeline.label: Roosevelt attacks the ‘nature fakers’
timeline.detail: The President, in a magazine interview, singled out the fight between the bulldog and the wolf-dog as the kind of thing no naturalist could believe.

timeline.label: London replies in ‘The Other Animals’
timeline.detail: Published in Collier’s in September, the essay defends his dogs as creatures of instinct and simple reasoning rather than of human thought.

timeline.label: London dies at Glen Ellen
timeline.detail: He was forty, and had published some fifty books in seventeen years.

timeline.label: First film adaptation
timeline.detail: A silent feature built around the dog star Strongheart, beginning a long line of screen versions.

timeline.label: A Soviet film version
timeline.detail: London’s standing as a socialist author made him one of the most widely read Americans in the Soviet Union, and the novel was filmed there soon after the war.

timeline.label: The Disney live-action film
timeline.detail: It enlarges the human story, gives the dog a young prospector for a companion and leaves out California and Jim Hall altogether.

timeline.label: An animated feature
timeline.detail: A French-made animated version told largely from the animal’s side, released internationally by a streaming service.

places.name: Mackenzie River
places.note: The country of Grey Beaver’s people. The cub is born beside a small stream that flows into it in summer, and the camp’s canoes and sleds move along it.

places.name: Great Slave Lake
places.note: Where Three Eagles is bound when he takes Kiche aboard his canoe in payment of Grey Beaver’s debt.

places.name: Fort Yukon, Alaska
places.note: The old Hudson’s Bay Company post at the mouth of the Porcupine, just under the Arctic Circle, where White Fang sees his first white men and is sold for whisky.

places.name: Dawson City, Yukon
places.note: Where the Fighting Wolf is exhibited in a cage for fifty cents in gold dust and fought in the woods outside town, out of sight of the mounted police.

places.name: San Francisco
places.note: The landing place from the North, all cable cars and towering buildings — and the slum in which Jim Hall was a child.

places.name: Santa Clara Valley, California
places.note: Sierra Vista, Judge Scott’s estate, lies here, in the same valley as the Judge Miller’s place from which Buck was stolen in the earlier book.

places.name: San Quentin State Prison
places.note: Where Jim Hall spends three years in the incorrigible cell, an iron tomb, before killing three guards and escaping.

criticalViews.position: The novel as a demonstration of environmental determinism
criticalViews.summary: On this reading White Fang is a thesis novel and an unusually honest one. London announces that heredity is clay and environment the modeller, runs his subject through four environments to show four characters, and extends the finding to a camp cook and a convict. The happy ending is then an argument for reform: change the conditions and you change the creature, whether the creature is a wolf or a slum child.
criticalViews.counter: The book will not live by its own rule. Beauty Smith is declared not responsible and then punched to applause, and the one human being who most resembles the hero is killed by him without a word of regret from anyone.

criticalViews.position: The novel as a story of conquest presented as love
criticalViews.summary: A more sceptical reading attends to the vocabulary of gods, masters, fealty and allegiance, and to the ranking of white gods above Indian ones at Fort Yukon. What the book celebrates, on this account, is a wild thing taught to guard a rich family’s property and lie quiet on its lawn, with the teaching called love because it no longer needs a club. The hierarchy of races and owners is never questioned by the narrative, only felt as natural from below.
criticalViews.counter: The hierarchy is White Fang’s, and the narrator repeatedly marks the distance between what the dog believes and what is so. The supposedly superior gods include the book’s most degraded human being, and the Judge’s household is shown to rest on a false conviction.

criticalViews.position: The lesser companion to The Call of the Wild
criticalViews.summary: A long-standing judgement holds that the second book is the weaker: longer, more explanatory, its thesis stated where Buck’s was dramatised, and its ending a retreat from the earlier novel’s nerve. Buck’s going wild has the force of myth, while White Fang’s coming tame ends in a drawing-room, with ladies applauding.
criticalViews.counter: The comparison mistakes a different subject for a failure. Submission, dependence and the making of a personality by other people are harder and less flattering matters than escape, and the Indian-camp chapters treat them with a patience the shorter book has no room for.

essayQuestions.question: ‘The clay of him had been so moulded.’ How far does White Fang hold to its own account of character?
essayQuestions.focus: Heredity, environment and the limits of the thesis
plan: Set out the theory as stated in Part 3, Chapter 6 — heredity as clay, environment as modeller — and note the hedged, lecturing voice in which it arrives.
Follow the refrain through its returns: Beauty Smith not responsible, the men at the cage as environment, the thumb of circumstance that is Weedon Scott, the soft clay of Jim Hall.
Test it against what the book gives as inherited: fear as a legacy, the knowledge of the throat, Collie’s instinct about wolves, Kiche answering her name.
Examine the places where the narrative’s sympathies break the rule — the pleasure taken in Scott’s fists, the unmourned death of Hall.
Conclude on the plummet and the deeps: whether love, as the book describes it, is something pressed on to the clay or something found inside it.

essayQuestions.question: How does London use the idea of men as gods, and what does it allow him to say?
essayQuestions.focus: Power, worship and the animal point of view
plan: Begin with the power of dead things in Part 3, Chapter 1: godhead defined from underneath, as command over sticks, stones and fire.
Read the long sentence on the god that stands on its hind-legs and is good to eat, and what it implies about human religion.
Trace the covenant: liberty exchanged for a flesh-and-blood god, and the admission that leaning on another is easier than standing alone.
Consider the ranking of gods at Fort Yukon and in San Francisco, and how far the narrator shares the dog’s scale of value.
End with Sierra Vista, where divinity means rules about chickens, and ask whether the metaphor has been domesticated along with the wolf.

essayQuestions.question: Why does a novel called White Fang spend its first three chapters on two men and a coffin?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, the displaced opening and the companion book
plan: Describe Part 1 as a complete tale in itself: six dogs, three cartridges, the she-wolf as decoy, Henry in his ring of fire.
Show what it establishes before the hero exists: the Wild as an enemy of movement, and the law of meat seen from the side of the eaten.
Consider the she-wolf’s double role, killer in Part 1 and mother in Part 2, and how the join changes the reader’s sympathies.
Compare the opening of The Call of the Wild, which begins with its hero and a newspaper; consider why the reversed journey needs a different door.
Set the last page against the first — sun for frost, stillness chosen for stillness imposed — and decide whether the structure closes a circle or abandons one.

essayQuestions.question: Is the ending of White Fang a fulfilment or a defeat?
essayQuestions.focus: Part 5, Jim Hall and the cost of the tame
plan: Gather the evidence for fulfilment: the broken window, the single-hearted love, laughter learned at last, the puppies in the sun.
Gather the evidence for cost: control and restraint as the chief demand of civilisation, the vague longings for snow, the nightmares of cable cars.
Read Jim Hall closely as the hero’s double, down to the cage, the brutal keeper and the teeth at a throat, and ask what it means that White Fang kills him.
Weigh the title the women give him, Blessed Wolf, and the Judge’s insistence that no mere dog could have done it.
Compare Buck’s ending at the head of a pack, and decide what each book thinks an animal is for.

discussionQuestions: White Fang could have stayed in the woods when the camp moved. Why does London make the return to Grey Beaver a choice?
The narrator says Beauty Smith is not responsible for what he is. Does the chapter that contains that sentence believe it?
Collie is the one member of the household who is right about White Fang. What is the novel doing by letting her be right and overruled?
Grey Beaver never pets his dog and never beats him without cause; Scott does both more warmly. Which of them does the book present as the better master, and on what grounds?
Jim Hall was innocent of the crime he was sentenced for. Why does London tell us so just before White Fang kills him?
Read beside The Call of the Wild, does this book answer the earlier one, correct it, or lose an argument with it?

related.why: The companion book, running the other way: a judge’s dog from the same Californian valley taken north and released into the pack.
A close reading of the hunt in which Buck feels the summit of life, for comparison with the cub’s joy in the play of his muscles.
Another creature made ferocious by the treatment he receives, with the same question about where the blame lies.
American naturalism applied to a boy under fire, with instinct and environment measured just as coldly.
Crane’s indifferent sea is a close relation of London’s Wild, which hates movement and laughs at effort.
Published two years later and the opposite experiment: animals given speech, waistcoats and houses rather than instinct and owners.
